Lessons.Title: Solving Systems by Elimination (Part 3)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: multiply one or both equations by nonzero numbers to create cancelling coefficients, solve a linear system and explain why it preserves all solutions. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L16, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/16/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source's crucial advance is scaled elimination, not addition alone. Publisher Addressing HSA-REI.C.5 and HSA-REI.C.6.

Original system 2x+3y=13 and 5x−2y=4. Multiplying first equality by 2 gives 4x+6y=26; multiplying second by 3 gives 15x−6y=12. Adding yields 19x=38, so x=2 and y=3. Both multipliers are nonzero; each scaled equation represents the same line as its predecessor.

Compare efficient alternatives: for x+2y=11 and 3x−2y=9, adding directly cancels y, giving 4x=20 and x=5, y=3. For 2x+3y=13,5x−2y=4, direct addition doesn't cancel, which motivates nonzero scaling. Graph the original and scaled lines on labelled axes to explain their identical solution sets.

Student task: choose a multiplier rather than copy an unexamined recipe, solve both systems, explain why multiplying by zero would be invalid, and check the resulting ordered pairs. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): suitable multiplier, correct elimination, proper full-system verification, and logical justification that all solutions were preserved.

KeyConcepts.Title: Strategic scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply all terms of an equation by the same fixed nonzero factor to match opposing coefficients.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a common multiple to cancel a variable.
KeyConcepts.Example: Multiply 3y by 2 and −2y by 3 to obtain +6y and −6y.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent line
KeyConcepts.Definition: Nonzero scaling preserves exactly the same line and solution set.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The factor must not be zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Combined-system verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: Solving a derived equation gives candidates; verify in the original system.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use the original unscaled equations for final checks.

WorkedExamples.Title: Scale both equations to eliminate y
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve 2x+3y=13 and 5x−2y=4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both original equations true; multipliers nonzero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize direct cancellation
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve x+2y=11 and 3x−2y=9.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Direct cancellation needs no scaling here.

WorkedExamples.Title: Show zero scaling loses information
WorkedExamples.Question: Does 0×(2x+3y=13) preserve its original line?
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: The original equation restricts the plane to a line.
The two equations are not equivalent.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; multiplying an equation by zero loses the original constraint.

CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply every left-side term and the right side by the same nonzero number.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Eliminating a variable but forgetting the other original constraint
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One reduced equation cannot identify the full ordered pair.

SummaryPoints: Use nonzero multipliers to create canceling coefficients.
Scaled equations represent the same line.
After adding, verify both original equations.
A teacher must evaluate multiplier-choice reasoning, not only the final pair.
